units.title: Boolean Reasoning and Logic Gates
units.description: Translate truth tables and Boolean expressions into simple, composable gate-level behavior.
units.content:
Digital logic represents information with two abstract values, 0 and 1. Real circuits map these values to voltage ranges, but Boolean algebra lets us reason about intended behavior without beginning with transistor physics. A truth table is the most direct specification for a small logic function: list every input combination and the required output. For n independent one-bit inputs there are 2^n rows, so tables are practical for a few inputs and useful as references for tests.

The basic operations are NOT, AND, and OR. NOT inverts one bit; AND is 1 only when every operand is 1; OR is 1 when at least one operand is 1. XOR is 1 when its inputs differ, and XNOR is 1 when they agree. NAND and NOR invert AND and OR. Operations compose: parentheses and operator precedence matter, so use parentheses to communicate intent. A two-input selector, for example, is (s AND d1) OR ((NOT s) AND d0). When s is 1 the first term passes d1; when s is 0 the second term passes d0.

Boolean identities simplify logic without changing its truth table. De Morgan's laws state that NOT(A AND B) equals (NOT A) OR (NOT B), and NOT(A OR B) equals (NOT A) AND (NOT B). These transformations help match available gates or check an expression. In RTL, `&`, `|`, `^`, and `~` are bitwise operators; vector forms operate independently at each bit. Logical operators such as `&&` and `!` instead interpret operands as truth values, so choose deliberately. Four-state simulation also includes X and Z; these model unknown and high-impedance conditions, not additional Boolean answers. Start from a two-state truth table, then use simulation to expose unknowns and incomplete assumptions. A correct implementation has an explicit relationship between every input and output. Small truth tables also make exhaustive verification affordable and support code review: a reviewer can compare each row with the RTL rather than trusting an informal verbal description.
keyPoints: A truth table enumerates all 2^n combinations of n one-bit inputs.
AND requires all inputs to be 1; OR requires at least one; XOR detects differing bits.
Parentheses make compound Boolean intent and precedence explicit.
Bitwise operators act per bit; logical operators reduce operands to truth values.
X in simulation signals unknown or undriven behavior that deserves investigation.

units.title: Number Systems, Widths, and Signed Values
units.description: Represent values precisely in binary RTL and reason about width, overflow, and signed interpretation.
units.content:
Hardware stores bit patterns; decimal values are interpretations of those patterns. A binary vector of width W has 2^W possible patterns. Unsigned interpretation ranges from 0 through 2^W−1. Two's-complement signed interpretation uses the same patterns but assigns the most significant bit as a negative-weight sign bit, giving a range from −2^(W−1) through 2^(W−1)−1. Four-bit 1111 is 15 unsigned but −1 signed. The bits alone do not determine meaning; declarations, expression sizing, and casts establish it.

Widths are functional design choices. An addition of two W-bit unsigned operands can require W+1 bits to preserve carry. If the result is assigned to only W bits, carry is discarded and arithmetic wraps modulo 2^W. Extend operands before the operation when the extra bit matters, as in `{1'b0,a} + {1'b0,b}`. Signed operands should be extended by replicating their sign bit, not by adding zero. Mixing signed and unsigned values can change comparisons and extension behavior; keep related operands at deliberate widths and signedness, and use explicit casts when conversion is intended. Sized literals such as `4'd9` make intent clearer than unsized values.

Hexadecimal is compact binary: one hex digit corresponds to four bits. Binary and hex are useful for masks and bit fields, while decimal is convenient for quantities. Fixed-point values also use integer bit patterns, but a design convention assigns some bits fractional weight; arithmetic does not automatically know the decimal point. For any arithmetic ask: what is operand width, what is signedness, how wide is the expression, and what should happen on overflow? Tests should include zero, maximum unsigned values, and signed extrema. Those cases reveal truncation or mistaken interpretation. Range calculations should precede declaration choices: a quantity needing values 0 through 100 requires at least seven unsigned bits, since six bits reach only 63. Choosing the minimum sufficient width saves resources, while margin should be justified by interface growth. Keep a bit-level calculation alongside decimal expectations when debugging arithmetic.
keyPoints: Unsigned W-bit values range 0 through 2^W−1.
Signed two’s-complement W-bit values range −2^(W−1) through 2^(W−1)−1.
Two unsigned W-bit operands need W+1 result bits to preserve carry.
Narrow assignment truncates high bits; unsigned overflow wraps modulo 2^W.
Extend operands deliberately and avoid accidental signed/unsigned mixing.

units.title: Combinational RTL and Selection Logic
units.description: Describe complete combinational functions with continuous assignments and complete procedural blocks.
units.content:
Combinational logic has no memory: outputs are functions only of current inputs. A continuous assignment such as `assign y = ...;` naturally expresses simple combinational behavior. For alternatives, an `always_comb` block with `if` or `case` may be clearer. The key requirement is completeness: every output assigned procedurally must receive a value on every possible path. If a path omits an assignment, hardware must retain the previous value, implying a latch. Latches can be intentional, but an accidental latch usually means the specification or code is incomplete.

A multiplexer selects one of several data inputs. A decoder activates an output based on an encoded input. A `case` statement is suitable for either if all relevant choices and a safe default are covered. In combinational `case`, assign defaults before branching, or ensure every branch assigns every output. `always_comb` communicates intent and adds checks beyond a generic procedural block, but does not excuse incomplete assignments. Avoid assigning one signal in multiple procedural processes; that creates ambiguous ownership and potentially conflicting drivers.

Blocking assignments (`=`) are generally used in combinational procedural code because statements execute in order, allowing later expressions to use earlier temporary values. Nonblocking assignments (`<=`) are generally used in edge-triggered sequential logic. Hardware is inferred from behavior, and simulation scheduling affects what a testbench observes in a time step. A concise combinational block can assign a default then override selected cases. For a mux, verify every select encoding; for a decoder, check active and inactive outputs. Consider unknown select values: a default can avoid accidental propagation but must match intended safety policy. Good RTL is synthesizable and easy to audit against a truth table. Avoid combinational feedback loops, which may fail to settle or infer unsupported logic. Naming signals by role and keeping selection logic readable helps debugging and maintenance.
keyPoints: Combinational outputs depend on present inputs, not stored history.
Every output needs an assignment on every path to avoid unintended latches.
Use always_comb for procedural combinational logic and case for selection.
A default assignment makes output behavior complete.
One procedural variable should have one clear owning process.

units.title: Arithmetic Datapaths and Simple ALUs
units.description: Build synthesizable arithmetic and logic datapaths with explicit widths, operation selection, and corner-case checks.
units.content:
A datapath transforms values; an arithmetic logic unit (ALU) selects among arithmetic and bitwise operations. Begin with a contract: operand widths, signedness, operation encodings, result width, and behavior for unsupported controls. These decisions prevent reliance on truncation or assumptions. In this example, two four-bit unsigned operands produce a five-bit addition result so carry is preserved. Subtraction uses an explicitly extended expression; a design might instead use a signed result or expose a borrow flag. State the choice and test it.

A `case` maps operation codes to results. Assign a default before the case to define a combinational output for unsupported codes. The default is not a substitute for defining the external protocol: decide whether invalid codes produce zero, an error flag, or are excluded by an invariant. Bitwise AND and XOR preserve operand width; arithmetic may need extra bits. Mixing vectors and scalars requires care because expression sizing and signedness determine evaluation. Flags such as zero and carry need precise definitions. An unsigned carry-out is not the same as signed overflow.

Combinational datapaths have no internal cycle latency; outputs settle after inputs and propagation. Larger datapaths may have long critical paths, so designers sometimes pipeline by inserting registers. That changes latency and requires control/data alignment; it is not merely syntax. First make behavior correct and explicit, then consider timing. Tests should exercise every operation, zero operands, maximum values, equal operands for subtraction, and invalid codes. Reference calculations should use enough bits to avoid repeating the implementation's truncation bug. Mathematical and bit-vector operations are related but not identical: modulo arithmetic, signed range, and result slicing determine actual hardware behavior. Good datapath design specifies both.
keyPoints: Define widths, signedness, result width, and operation encodings in the interface.
Addition may need a carry bit beyond operand width.
Unsigned carry and signed overflow are different conditions.
Use a complete case/default for combinational operation selection.
Pipelining improves timing at the cost of latency and control alignment.

units.title: Flip-Flops, Resets, and Enables
units.description: Model state changes on clock edges using synthesizable sequential RTL and understand reset and enable behavior.
units.content:
Sequential logic stores information. A flip-flop samples its input at an active clock edge and holds the sampled value until another edge or reset event. In SystemVerilog an edge-triggered block is conventionally written with `always_ff`; use nonblocking assignments (`<=`) for state updates. Nonblocking assignments schedule updates together at the end of the time step, modeling registers sampling old values simultaneously. This avoids order-dependent behavior when several registers update on the same edge.

A synchronous reset is examined only at the active edge. An asynchronous reset can affect state independently of the clock and appears in the event control, commonly `@(posedge clk or posedge rst)`. Reset polarity must be unambiguous in its name and logic. Reset establishes a known starting state; it should not be added mechanically to every data path. Some implementation flows prefer particular reset structures, and asynchronous reset deassertion near a clock edge can cause metastability unless release is synchronized. Choose reset style intentionally and test exact timing.

An enable holds state when inactive: no assignment in the sequential branch means the register retains its value. That retention is a flip-flop feature, not a combinational latch, because the process is edge-triggered. Consider reset priority relative to enable. The example prioritizes reset, then enable, then hold. A common bug is assigning new data in the wrong branch. Another is using blocking assignment for state and making simulation depend on process ordering. A synchronous testbench should drive inputs before sampling edge, wait for the edge and nonblocking update, then inspect outputs. Check both change and hold and verify reset assertion and release according to the interface.

An uninitialized register may appear X in simulation until reset or known assignment, even if a technology has a particular power-up behavior. Do not rely on accidental initialization unless the target guarantees it. Reset sequencing is part of integration: reset should be asserted and released safely, and different clock domains need separate synchronization. These distinctions make state behavior portable and predictable.
keyPoints: always_ff at a clock edge describes state updates.
Use nonblocking assignments for edge-triggered register updates.
Synchronous reset is sampled at edge; asynchronous reset is event driven.
A disabled register holds state when no sequential assignment is made.
Document reset polarity and priority; safely synchronize asynchronous reset release.

units.title: Counters, Registers, and Cycle-Level Timing
units.description: Design counters and reason about modulo behavior, enables, reset, and cycle boundaries.
units.content:
A register stores a vector across cycles. A counter is a register whose next value derives from its current value, commonly by adding one. An N-bit unsigned counter naturally wraps after 2^N−1 because only N low bits are retained. This modulo behavior is useful for periodic sequences but is not saturating behavior. If an application requires a non-power-of-two limit, compare against terminal count and explicitly choose whether to return to zero, hold, or signal completion.

The example implements a four-bit synchronous-clear, enabled counter. At a rising edge, clear has priority; otherwise asserted enable increments; otherwise count holds. This priority is part of the design contract and should be apparent in code and tests. Avoid using a derived counter bit as another block's clock unless architecture explicitly permits it; use an enable pulse in one clock domain instead. Generated clocks complicate timing analysis and clock-domain crossing.

Cycle-level reasoning distinguishes values before an edge, sampled values at the edge, and updated values afterward. Nonblocking assignments schedule new state after edge-triggered processes evaluate, so a testbench checks just after the edge. Current count is state; next count is a combinational calculation sampled into state. In larger pipelines, operations may take several cycles and valid/ready signals must align with data. This small counter illustrates synchronous design: state changes occur at the common clock boundary.

Boundary tests are essential. Check clear overrides enable, disabled count holds, enabled count increments, and 15 wraps to zero. A test that counts only zero through three never discovers rollover defects. For wider counters, use a parameter or focused setup to reach rollover without a long simulation, while keeping the test representative. Counters consume resources and can toggle many bits; choose width from required range rather than using an unnecessarily large integer. For an external pulse, define whether it is one cycle wide and whether it occurs on reaching or leaving terminal count.
keyPoints: An N-bit unsigned counter wraps modulo 2^N.
The example gives synchronous clear priority over enable.
With enable and clear low, a register holds state.
Check state after active edge and NBA update.
Use clock enables instead of casual generated clocks.

units.title: Finite-State Machines
units.description: Represent control behavior with explicit state, next-state logic, outputs, and reset transitions.
units.content:
A finite-state machine (FSM) is a sequential controller with a finite set of states. Its next state depends on current state and inputs; outputs may depend only on state (Moore) or on state and current inputs (Mealy). Start with a state diagram or transition table, including reset behavior and meaning of each input sequence. Only then translate behavior into RTL. State names should describe behavior, not arbitrary bit patterns. Enumerated `typedef enum logic` states improve clarity and allow synthesis to choose encoding.

A common RTL structure separates a state register from combinational next-state logic. The `always_ff` block updates state on a clock edge and reset establishes an initial state. The `always_comb` block begins with `next_state = state`, then overrides it for transitions. This default defines a hold transition and prevents incomplete assignment. Outputs can be decoded separately. For a Mealy output, assign a default low and assert it only for a matching state/input condition. This can reduce latency versus a Moore output, but makes outputs respond to input changes between edges and can create timing or glitch concerns.

The example detects two consecutive sampled ones. It has idle and seen-one states. In idle, a one advances to seen-one; in seen-one, another one produces a pulse and remains in seen-one, so a run of ones produces a pulse on each sample after the first. A zero returns to idle. The output is Mealy because it depends on current state and input. Behavior is specified at sampling edges; real hardware still requires input setup and hold.

FSM verification should test transitions, not just outputs in one state. Include reset from a non-reset state, each transition, overlapping sequences, and unexpected-state recovery if defined. Simulation X can reveal uninitialized state, but synthesized encoding and recovery vary by tool and constraints. Never assume a particular enum encoding. Keep reset and output semantics explicit, and drive inputs away from sampling edge to avoid races. For external asynchronous inputs, add synchronizers before the FSM; state logic alone does not eliminate metastability.
keyPoints: An FSM has finite state, next-state function, and defined outputs.
Moore outputs depend on state; Mealy outputs depend on state and current inputs.
Separate sequential state storage from combinational next-state logic.
Set combinational defaults to avoid inferred latches.
Test transitions and sequences at clock boundaries.

test.objective: Check detector pulse on second consecutive sampled one and reset/zero transitions.
test.integrationAssumptions: Compile with beginner07. Drive at falling edges, check Mealy output, then let the following rising edge sample the input.

units.title: Testbench Fundamentals and Self-Checking Verification
units.description: Create deterministic SystemVerilog testbenches that drive inputs, compare expected behavior, and report failures.
units.content:
A testbench is a simulation environment, not hardware intended for synthesis. It instantiates a design under test (DUT), drives inputs, observes outputs, and decides whether behavior matches specification. A useful testbench is self-checking: it reports failure automatically with enough context to reproduce it and calls `$fatal` or otherwise signals nonzero status. Waveforms help diagnosis, but visual inspection alone makes regressions easy to miss.

For a combinational DUT, drive input patterns, allow a small simulation delay or use deliberate synchronization, then compare outputs with an independent expected value. For a sequential DUT, drive controls before the active edge, wait for the edge, then allow nonblocking assignments to commit before checking state. Avoid driving and checking in the same scheduling region as DUT update; this can create races. Initialize testbench variables deliberately and establish reset before relying on sequential state.

Case inequality (`!==`) is useful in four-state simulation because it flags X or Z as a mismatch instead of allowing an unknown comparison result to pass silently. Test meaningful boundaries and control combinations, not merely a happy path. Exhaustive tests are affordable for small input spaces; larger spaces benefit from directed cases and constrained random testing. A reference model should be simple and independent enough not to copy the DUT's bug. Include a timeout so a stuck simulation fails instead of hanging. Print PASS only after every check succeeds.

The example is a two-bit equality comparator. Its testbench iterates over every possible pair, calculates expected equality using loop variables, and checks the DUT. This demonstrates exhaustive verification. In larger projects, separate stimulus, checking, and coverage into tasks or classes, but preserve reproducibility with fixed random seed and log failing inputs. Verification does not prove physical timing or analog properties; it checks modeled function and complements lint, synthesis, and timing analysis. A clear completion condition lets automation distinguish pass from incomplete run.
keyPoints: A testbench instantiates DUT, drives stimulus, observes outputs, and checks expected behavior.
Drive sequential inputs before edge and sample after NBA updates.
Case inequality (`!==`) detects mismatches involving X or Z.
Use directed cases or exhaustive enumeration for small input spaces.
Add failure context and timeout to make regressions actionable.

units.title: RTL Tool Flow: Simulate, Lint, Synthesize
units.description: Use simulation, lint, synthesis, and timing analysis as complementary stages in a reproducible workflow.
units.content:
An RTL tool flow transforms a behavioral description into an implementation while checking different error classes at different stages. Source files and parameters are assembled into a design with selected top module and target configuration. Lint examines suspicious constructs, width mismatches, incomplete assignments, unused signals, and style problems. It does not prove functional correctness, but finds issues before simulation or synthesis. Treat warnings as information to understand, not noise to suppress without review.

Simulation executes RTL with a testbench. It checks functional behavior for selected or exhaustive sequences and exposes X propagation or reset mistakes. It depends on stimulus and checks; a clean run cannot establish that every behavior was tested. Synthesis interprets synthesizable RTL and maps it into logic cells or FPGA resources. It can reveal unsupported constructs, infer unexpected latches, and report resource use. Successful synthesis does not guarantee correct function or timing closure.

Implementation tools may place and route mapped logic. Static timing analysis (STA) checks paths against clock and I/O constraints without requiring simulated vectors. Correct constraints are essential: missing or unrealistic clocks can make results misleading. A design can simulate correctly but fail timing; it can meet timing while implementing the wrong function. Use complementary evidence. Record tool versions, source lists, top module, defines, parameters, and constraints so a run is reproducible. Keep generated artifacts separate from source and inspect warnings and reports.

A disciplined loop is edit, lint, focused simulation, expand tests, synthesize, inspect inferred hardware and warnings, then evaluate timing after implementation. If a test fails, reduce it to a reproducible vector and fix specification or RTL instead of masking the symptom. The example is a parity reduction, a tiny synthesizable target for simulation and synthesis sanity checks. Its testbench checks all eight three-bit values. Tools answer different questions; no single green status replaces review. Version-controlled scripts and constraints reduce hidden environment differences and make regressions repeatable.
keyPoints: Lint flags suspicious constructs but does not prove function.
Simulation checks modeled behavior for supplied stimulus and assertions.
Synthesis maps RTL and exposes unsupported or unexpectedly inferred structures.
STA depends on accurate clock and I/O constraints.
Keep sources, top, parameters, defines, tool versions, and constraints reproducible.

units.title: Parameterized Modules and Reusable RTL
units.description: Write reusable hardware with parameters while guarding widths, boundaries, and elaboration-time assumptions.
units.content:
Parameters let one RTL module describe a family of hardware instances. A parameter is resolved during elaboration, before simulation or synthesis of the chosen instance; it is not a runtime input and does not add a programmable register. Width parameters avoid copying nearly identical code for each size. Use named parameter overrides at instantiation so intent remains clear. A parameterized module must be checked at important configurations, especially minimum legal width and boundaries.

The example counter uses `parameter int WIDTH = 4` and declares count as `[WIDTH-1:0]`. This is valid only when WIDTH is positive; zero or negative width creates an invalid range. Reusable IP should document supported values and, where practical, issue an elaboration-time assertion for invalid choices. Natural rollover depends on width. Unsized constants in parameterized arithmetic can introduce width or signedness surprises, so use sized casts or expressions matching parameter width. `$clog2` is common for address widths, but `$clog2(1)` is zero; handle the singleton case deliberately.

Parameterized code should not merely compile at the default. Instantiate multiple widths in tests and include a small width so rollover is reached quickly. Check elaborated port widths and behavior including enable hold and reset. Parameters affect timing, resource use, and implementation choices; a generic description does not guarantee every instance meets the same performance target. If parameters select features or operation modes, test each supported combination rather than assuming one configuration represents all.

Reusable modules benefit from clear interfaces and self-contained behavior. Avoid hidden dependencies on global macros or a particular parent module. Keep parameters named, document legal ranges, and make defaults useful but not magical. Compile-time configuration and generate blocks are powerful but increase elaboration complexity; use them when they improve reuse or clarity. A good parameterized component has defined behavior for every supported configuration and tests that prove variation is real, not merely syntactic. Consider whether output width, counter limit, and reset value all scale coherently when width changes.
keyPoints: Parameters configure hardware at elaboration, not runtime.
Document legal parameter ranges and guard vector bounds against invalid widths.
Test minimum and representative larger configurations, not only default.
Derived widths such as $clog2(1) need deliberate handling.
Resources and timing can vary across parameter sizes.
